headline: Lenders Catch Up to Bond Selloff; Rates Near 7.5%
tileReason: The daily 30-year average reached 7.50% Friday as lenders caught up with Thursday's late bond selloff; the 10-year yield is easing slightly this morning after a weak factory survey, ahead of Fed Chair Warsh's noon remarks.
takeaway:
Rates ended last week at their highest in over a month. The daily 30-year average rose to 7.50% Friday from 7.42% Thursday, a third straight increase that adds up to about 0.32% since Monday, Nov 9, and wipes out most of October's improvement. Other trackers are lower but moving the same way: Mortgage Research Center shows about 7.32% this morning, and Zillow showed 7.27% Friday.

Friday's jump was lenders catching up, not a new selloff. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, was roughly flat Friday and finished around 5.13% to 5.15% depending on the source. But bonds had weakened late Thursday, after most lenders had already set their rates for the day, so that move showed up in Friday morning's pricing instead.

This morning brings a little relief. The 10-year yield has eased to about 5.11% to 5.14%, and a New York-area factory survey released this morning came in at 7.8, far below the 17.6 economists expected; softer economic news like that tends to help rates. Oil is slightly lower too, though Iranian drone attacks on a U.S. base in Bahrain keep energy prices jumpy. Mortgage News Daily's index for today posts this afternoon.

A December Fed hike is all but locked in. Futures markets, where traders bet on the Fed's next move, now put the odds of a quarter-point increase in the Fed's short-term rate on Dec 9 at about 91% to 94%, with the rest on a bigger half-point move. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at noon Eastern today and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack this afternoon, so any hint of more increases after December could push rates up again.

Lenders still have some cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.15% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 12, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That extra room means lenders don't have to pass along every bit of a bond-market selloff, which is part of why mortgage rates have risen less than Treasury yields this month.

This week brings several tests. October retail sales come Tuesday morning, with Nvidia's earnings after the close, and the minutes of the Fed's October meeting come Wednesday afternoon. After that: the Fed's preferred inflation measure on Nov 25, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via BigGo Finance and TipRanks (Nov 16); Trading Economics (Nov 16); Friday reading CME FedWatch via FXEmpire (Nov 13)
fedOdds.note: These are the odds of a quarter-point hike. BigGo Finance, citing CME FedWatch, shows 91% to 94%, with 6% to 9% on a half-point move, so a hike of some size is close to 100%. TipRanks cites about 94% and Trading Economics above 93%. Friday's reading after the wholesale inflation report was about 90%.

drivers.title: Lenders caught up to Thursday's late selloff
drivers.text: Bonds weakened late Thursday after most lenders had already set their rates, so lenders raised rates Friday morning even though the 10-year yield barely moved that day. That pushed the daily 30-year average up 0.08% to 7.50%, its third straight increase.

drivers.title: A December Fed hike is close to certain
drivers.text: Futures markets put the odds of a quarter-point hike on Dec 9 at about 91% to 94%, and Governor Christopher Waller said last week a bigger half-point move should be on the table if inflation keeps building. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling.

drivers.title: Inflation still running hot
drivers.text: October consumer prices beat forecasts for the third month in a row, and wholesale prices are up 6.5% from a year ago, the most since 2022. Bond investors demand higher yields when inflation eats into what their interest is worth, and mortgage rates follow.

drivers.title: Weak factory survey and slightly lower yields this morning
drivers.text: The New York Fed's factory survey fell to 7.8 in November from 25.5, far below the 17.6 expected, and the 10-year yield slipped to about 5.11% to 5.14%. Signs of a cooling economy tend to pull yields and mortgage rates down.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.15% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 12, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields without raising rates as much.

outlook.baseSource: Mortgage News Daily, Nov 13 close (latest available)
outlook.basis: The odds are close to even, with a slight lean higher. At 7.50%, mortgage rates have now caught up with most of last week's bond selloff, and the 10-year Treasury yield is easing a little this morning. Working against borrowers: a December Fed hike is close to fully expected, inflation reports keep running hot, and Fed officials keep talking about more increases. In borrowers' favor: this morning's factory survey was much weaker than expected, mortgage rates still sit unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.15% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), and home sales are slowing. Big swing events: Chair Warsh's remarks today, Tuesday's retail sales, Wednesday's Fed minutes, the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision, Dec 10 consumer prices and oil headlines tied to Iran.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average reached 7.50% Friday after three straight increases, its highest in over a month, though still below the 7.6%-plus levels of early October. Bond yields are easing a bit this morning, but Fed Chair Warsh speaks today and a December Fed hike is close to certain. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates gave back most of October's improvement last week, and October home sales fell 5.5%, so buyers are feeling the pinch again. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out heading into the holidays.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates climbed to about 7.5% last week as hot inflation and a widely expected December Fed hike pushed bond yields above 5.1%.
